Males of this species attain an identical ultimate body length of 49 cm [Li = 49 cm], reflecting a lack of pronounced sexual size dimorphism that is somewhat unusual among North American pit vipers. Both sexes experience a relatively rapid early growth phase, with individuals often reaching a snout-vent length of 35 cm [Lp = 35 cm] at the onset of puberty. This length corresponds to the attainment of sexual maturity, which typically occurs around two years of age based on mark-recapture data from wild populations. The consistency in pubertal size between the sexes suggests that energetic constraints on reaching reproductive size are similar for males and females in this species. Field studies have documented that individuals invest heavily in somatic growth during their first two active seasons before diverting resources toward gametogenesis and courtship behavior.

This early onset of exogenous feeding is critical because the yolk reserves are largely depleted by the time of emergence. Hatchlings possess a bright yellow tail tip that they use as a caudal lure to attract prey, a behavior that becomes less pronounced as they mature into the juvenile stage. The small body size at birth makes them vulnerable to a wide array of predators, including birds of prey, larger snakes, and mammalian mesopredators.

Gravid females exhibit a marked shift in thermoregulatory behavior, selecting cooler microhabitats that are thought to reduce metabolic stress on the developing embryos.
